buildings.role: The build library: dependency installation, transpilation, snapshotting, signing and artefact compression.
The fixture library the Jasmine suite loads: sample source files in each supported language, sample packages and prepared directories.
The shared UI component stylesheets bundled with the app, documented for theme authors in their own README.
The default UI theme, shipped as an ordinary Atom theme package of Less stylesheets with its own config schema.
The Electron main process: AtomApplication and window lifecycle, the command line parser, menus, the atom:// protocol, file recovery and auto-update.
The Azure Pipelines definitions that build, lint and release the app, with per-platform templates and artifact upload steps.
A bundled package that marks lines in the editor gutter added, edited or deleted since the last commit.
The editor model: buffers, cursors, selections and decorations, independent of how it is drawn.
Stylesheets for the editor chrome itself: the text editor, panes, docks, panels, cursors, title bar and workspace view.
The rendering half of the editor, which draws the model into the custom element.
Panes, docks and the item model behind everything the user sees in the window.
The global atom object: it wires together config, commands, packages, the workspace and every registry.
The settings system: schema, defaults, scoped overrides and persistence.
Tree-sitter powered syntax highlighting and indentation, the later of the two grammar engines.
One pane: an ordered list of items with one active item and at most one pending item, which is what the tab bar is drawn from.
Loads, activates and deactivates packages; the mechanism that made the editor hackable.
The left, right and bottom docks: edge containers that hold pane items and can be resized, animated open or hidden.
The older grammar engine: it tokenises lines with oniguruma regexes into the scoped tokens highlighting is driven from.
The open project: its root directories, the directory providers that supply them and the git repositories behind them; exposed as atom.project.
Normalises created, modified, deleted and renamed events from the native watchers into per-path subscriptions.
Holds every loaded grammar and picks one per file, choosing between the TextMate and tree-sitter language modes; exposed as atom.grammars.
Wraps git-utils to answer status, diff and head questions for a project directory, dispatching to the right submodule by path.
Associates listener functions with namespace:action commands through CSS selectors; keybindings and the command palette both resolve against it.
Loads and activates UI and syntax themes and compiles their Less through a cache; exposed as atom.themes.
The registry of active style sheets that atom-styles elements subscribe to and clone into their own contexts; exposed as atom.styles.
The renderer side of the Electron IPC boundary: window operations, folder pickers and settings updates are forwarded to the main process here.
Maps model objects to views through registered view providers, which is how a pane item becomes a DOM element.
The module every community package required; the stable API boundary of the editor.

ai.summary: Atom is an archived Electron text editor. src holds the editor core and the main process; the bundled first-party packages in packages are ordinary Atom packages that ship with the app. spec, script, resources and static carry the tests, the build pipeline, the installer assets and the stylesheets. The repository was archived in January 2023.

strengths: The extension model is applied to the editor itself: the bundled UI lives in packages as ordinary Atom packages rather than as special cases.
The public API is a real boundary, with exports re-exporting only the parts of Electron packages were meant to touch.
Specs mirror src file for file, so the intended unit of behaviour is easy to locate.
The whole release pipeline, including code signing and installers for three platforms, is checked into script rather than held by a build machine.
Build instructions, contribution guidance and an RFC archive are all committed in docs.
concerns: The repository is archived and has not been pushed to since January 2023; nothing here will be fixed.
Close to 1,000 issues and pull requests were open at the point the project was archived, so the tracker is a snapshot, not a queue.
CI ran on Azure Pipelines definitions under script/vsts, which no longer run; .github holds only issue bots, so the repository has no working build today.
src is a flat directory of over 100 files where the editor, the workspace and the grammar engines all sit at the same level.
Two grammar engines, the legacy TextMate path and tree-sitter, coexist in the core.
